source_caption_text:
Dwayne Michael Carter Jr., born in New Orleans in 1982, grew up in one of the toughest neighborhoods in the city. By 8 years old, he was already writing music. At 11, he signed his first record deal with Cash Money Records — becoming one of the youngest artists in hip‑hop history.

At 12, Wayne survived a self‑inflicted gunshot wound, an event he later revealed was a suicide attempt. A police officer named Robert Hoobler saved his life, and Wayne often credits that moment as the turning point that shaped his future.

Through the late ’90s and early 2000s, Wayne evolved from a Hot Boy into a solo powerhouse. His Dedication mixtapes, Tha Carter series, and relentless work ethic turned him into the face of mixtape culture. He didn’t just rap — he outworked everyone, recording constantly, experimenting with styles, and pushing boundaries.

By the time Tha Carter III dropped in 2008, Wayne was a global superstar. Grammy wins, record‑breaking sales, and a reputation as one of the most influential lyricists of his generation cemented his legacy.

He later founded Young Money, launching the careers of Drake and Nicki Minaj — two artists who would go on to dominate the next decade.

Today, Lil Wayne stands as a cultural icon:
a pioneer, a survivor, a mentor, and one of the most impactful rappers to ever touch a microphone. 🐐🔥
